newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Australian trade minister sees future in gold.
newsitem.headline: Australian trade minister sees future in gold.

text.p: The Australian government believes gold mining still has a future and that demand for the metal will increase in time after its recent drop in price, Australian trade minister Tim Fischer said on Tuesday.

"The Australian government believes there is a great future in gold mining in the southern hemisphere, Australia and South Africa," Fischer, who is leading a business delegation to South Africa, told a news conference in the east coast port city of Durban.
"The Australian government would like to encourage the future of gold mining," he said.

Last week the Reserve Bank of Australia announced that it had sold 167 tonnes of gold in the first six months of this year, triggering a wholesale sell-off of the metal to its lowest level in 12 years of around $318.
Fischer noted that it had been the Australian central bank's decision to sell two thirds of its gold reserves this year and not the government's.
He also noted that the actual sale by the Australian central bank had not prompted any slump in the gold price, but that the announcement had.
On top of previous disposals by the Belgian and Dutch central banks, the disclosure had unnerved already jittery investors, he said.
"In the longer term I am confident of the continued demand for gold," Fischer said, adding that he expected demand to emanate mainly from China.
"There is no doubt that China will become the largest economy in the course of the next century," he added.

Traders have said the gold price could fall below the $300 level, with some predicting a possible downside target of $287.25 -- a level last seen in 1985. This was based on the fear that other central banks could sell off some of the 35,000 tonnes held by government institutions around the world.
South Africa produces the majority of the world's gold with output last year of 495 tonnes. The U.S. is second, producing 329 tonnes in 1996, and Australia third with 289 tonnes last year.

On a total cost basis, analysts have said Australia produces about 40-45 percent of its gold below the current price, while at current levels about 60 percent of world production was being made at a loss.
Gold was fixed at $320.80 in London on Tuesday afternoon -- up from a 12-year low of $318 registered on Monday.
